pos: n. (the greatest of the Swiss city-states, which took the Reformation by the disputation and mandate of 1528 and carried it into the Pays de Vaud)
etymology: German Bern, from Bär, a bear, by the city's own tradition and arms; the town was founded on the peninsula of the Aare in 1191.
biblical_def: Bern was the largest territorial power of the old Swiss Confederation, a patrician city-state ruling a country from the Jura to the high Alps, and its decision settled the Reformation for western Switzerland. The city hesitated for years. It then did what the Swiss cities did: it called a public disputation, which sat in January 1528 with Zwingli, Bucer, Capito and Oecolampadius present, debated ten theses over nineteen days, and concluded for the Reformed side. The Reformation Mandate followed in February; the Mass was abolished, the images taken out of the minster, the monasteries dissolved and their revenues turned to schools and poor relief, and a church order set up under the city's own authority. In 1536 Bern conquered the Pays de Vaud from Savoy and introduced the Reformation there by the same means, a disputation at Lausanne and then a mandate. Bern subscribed the Second Helvetic Confession in 1566. The dictionary enters Bern because the Bernese settlement is the clearest instance of a Reformed church fully subject to its magistrate: the council appointed, paid, examined and disciplined the ministers, kept the keys of discipline in its own hand, and in 1559 expelled the ministers of Lausanne for saying that it should not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mandate as a command, an authoritative order; a canton as a small territory constituting a state; and a magistrate as a public civil officer invested with authority.
webster_full: MANDATE, n. [L. mandatum.] A command; an order, precept or injunction; a commission; an authoritative charge.
CANTON, n. [Fr.] A small portion or district of territory, constituting a distinct state or government, as in Switzerland.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it; a person clothed with power.
DISPUTATION, n. A contest in words or by arguments; a public exercise in argumentation, as before a council.
DISCIPLINE, n. Instruction and government; subjection to rules; correction; the system by which a church orders its members.

corruption_summary: Swiss city-state which took the Reformation by disputation and mandate in 1528, and which kept the keys of church discipline in its council's hand.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the Erastian settlement, and Bern is its classic Reformed instance. The doctrine the city established was substantially sound and the dictionary holds it; what the city also established was that the civil council is the final judge in the church—appointing and removing ministers, deciding who is admitted to the Supper, and treating excommunication as a magistrate's act. “the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) is a body with its own officers and its own discipline, given it by Christ and not by a council.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the distinction of the spheres which Bern denied in practice while confessing it on paper. The magistrate is “the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4) in the civil sphere, and his office is to protect the church and punish evildoers, not to admit or exclude at the Lord's table. The dictionary records that the Bernese council did much good—schools, poor relief, the clearing of the churches—and that the price it exacted was the church's liberty, which was paid in 1559.

pos: n. (Berchtold Haller, 1492–1536, the reformer of Bern)
etymology: Haller, a south German surname, from Hall, a salt-works; Berchtold, from Germanic beraht, bright, and wald, rule.
biblical_def: Berchtold Haller was a Swabian who came to Bern as a schoolmaster, became a canon and then the people's preacher at the minster, and carried the Reformation there over ten slow years. He was a cautious man and knew it, and his letters to Zwingli are a long record of a diffident minister asking a bolder one what to do; Zwingli replied with encouragement and sometimes with impatience. Haller preached from the Scriptures without immediately attacking the ceremonies, let the city's mind change under the preaching, and avoided the confrontations that would have ended his ministry before the council was ready. When the council at last called the disputation of January 1528 he was its principal author on the Reformed side, and when it was won he drew up the church order and the liturgy of the Bernese church and served it until his death in 1536. The dictionary enters Haller for his temperament, which is worth as much notice as a bolder man's courage. He was timid, he knew the city would not be driven, and his patience accomplished in Bern what a bolder man would have lost; and he is the standing answer to the assumption that the useful minister is always the fearless one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines diffident as distrustful of oneself, not confident; patience as the bearing of delay with calmness; and prudence as wisdom applied to practice.
webster_full: DIFFIDENT, adj. [L. diffidens.] Distrustful; wanting confidence; not confident; hesitating; modest; reserved.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of delays, afflictions or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
PRUDENCE, n. [L. prudentia.] Wisdom applied to practice; that discretion which guides us in the choice of means and ends.
CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; one who possesses a prebend in a cathedral or collegiate church.
LITURGY, n. All the prescribed services of a church; a formulary of public prayers and the order of worship.

corruption_summary: The reformer of Bern, a diffident preacher whose patience carried a cautious city over ten years to the disputation of 1528.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the cult of the bold minister: the assumption that faithfulness is measured by confrontation, and that a man who waits is compromising. Haller waited ten years, under criticism from his own side, and Bern was reformed. The dictionary does not make the opposite error either; there are hours when a man must speak at once and Luther at Worms is the pattern of them. The discernment between the two hours is what Scripture calls prudence, and it is a gift of the Spirit and not a want of nerve.

The principle to recover is in the apostle's own division of the labour: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6). The planter and the waterer are different men with different tempers and neither is the one who gives the increase. “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) includes the out-of-season hours, and also assumes there is such a thing as season, which a man must judge.

pos: n. (Johannes Haller, 1523–1575, dean of Bern, who brought the city to subscribe the Second Helvetic Confession)
etymology: Haller, a south German surname from Hall, a salt-works; Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Johannes Haller, no relation of Berchtold, was born in the Bernese Oberland, lost his father at the battle of Kappel, was raised and trained under Bullinger at Zurich, and served the Reformed congregation at Augsburg before the Interim drove him out. From 1552 until his death in 1575 he was dean of Bern, the senior minister of the Bernese church, and in that office he did the work the city most needed and least wanted. Bern had been theologically isolated: it had taken the Reformation in a Zwinglian form, quarrelled with Geneva and with its own Vaud ministers about discipline and about Calvin's doctrine of election, and suspected Zurich of leaning toward Geneva. Haller, trusted at Zurich and respected at Bern, worked patiently to bring the city into the common Reformed confession, and in 1566 Bern subscribed the Second Helvetic Confession, which Bullinger had drafted. He also had to manage the Bernese council, which held the discipline of the church in its own hand and had expelled the Lausanne ministers for disputing it. The dictionary enters him as the type of the churchman whose service is agreement—not compromise, since the confession he obtained was the fuller one, but the patient removal of the suspicion that had kept a great church apart from its brethren.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a confession as a formulary of the articles of faith; a dean as the second dignitary of a diocese or chapter; and concord as agreement between persons.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; the acknowledgment of a belief before witnesses.
DEAN, n. [L. decanus.] In England, the second dignitary of a diocese; in reformed churches, the presiding minister of a chapter or classis.
CONCORD, n. [L. concordia.] Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests; harmony.
ISOLATION, n. The state of being detached or separated from others of a like kind.
SUBSCRIBE, v.t. To write under; to sign with one's own hand; to assent to by signing one's name.

corruption_summary: Dean of Bern for twenty-three years, who brought an isolated and suspicious church to subscribe the Second Helvetic Confession in 1566.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the identification of all concord with compromise. What Haller obtained at Bern was not a lowest common formula but subscription to a full and particular confession, drafted at Zurich, which states election, the Supper and the ministry at length and leaves little undecided. The dictionary distinguishes sharply between agreement reached by stating the doctrine more fully, which is a gain, and agreement reached by stating it more vaguely, which is the ordinary modern instrument and is a loss.

The principle to recover is that confessional agreement between churches is a duty and not a luxury. “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) is one faith, and churches that hold it are obliged to say so to each other in words. Bern's long isolation did it no good: it bred the suspicion of Geneva which cost it Viret and the Lausanne academy, and it left the city's own ministers without the help of a wider body when the council overreached.

pos: n. (Bernese town of the Aargau; where the disputation with the Anabaptists was held in 1532)
etymology: German Zofingen, from a personal name Zofo with the Germanic -ingen, the people of Zofo; the town lies on the Wigger in the upper Aargau.
biblical_def: Zofingen is a small town of the Bernese Aargau, and it is remembered because in July 1532 the city of Bern held there a public disputation with the Anabaptists of its territory. This was unusual. The ordinary treatment of Anabaptists in the Reformed cantons was legal: banishment, fines, imprisonment, and in some cases death, and Zurich had drowned men for rebaptism within living memory. Bern instead summoned their representatives, gave them a safe conduct, and argued with them for nine days in the presence of the ministers and the council's deputies, on the church and its purity, the oath, the magistracy, the ban, and the baptism of infants. Both sides claimed the victory and the council afterwards continued its penal measures, so that the disputation did not settle anything; but it was an attempt to answer rather than simply to suppress. The dictionary enters Zofingen for the attempt, and because the record of the debate is one of the best sources for what the Swiss Brethren actually held in their own words, rather than as summarised by men who were prosecuting them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a safe conduct as a convoy or guard granted to a person; the ban as the sentence of excommunication; and rebaptism as a second baptism.
webster_full: SAFE-CONDUCT, n. That which gives a safe passage; a convoy or guard to protect a person in an enemy's country or in a hostile region.
BAN, n. [Sax. bannan.] A public proclamation; a curse or excommunication; interdiction; a sentence of exclusion.
ANABAPTIST, n. [Gr. again, and baptist.] One who holds the doctrine of the baptism of adults, or of the invalidity of infant baptism.
CONFERENCE, n. [Fr.] A discourse between two or more for the purpose of instruction or the settling of a question; a meeting for consultation.
SUPPRESS, v.t. To crush; to subdue; to put an end to; to prohibit the exercise of.

corruption_summary: Bernese Aargau town where the city argued nine days with its Anabaptists in 1532, under safe conduct, and then resumed its penal measures.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the punishment of a doctrine by the sword, and the dictionary names it against the Reformed cities as plainly as against Rome. Bern, Zurich and Basel used banishment, fines and in some cases death against men whose error, where it was error, was a matter for the church's discipline and not the magistrate's. The Zofingen disputation shows that the better course was available and was even attempted; the resumption of the penal measures afterwards shows what the cities actually relied on.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary's own position complicates this entry and it says so. On baptism it stands with the Swiss Brethren against Bern: “Then they that gladly received his word were baptized” (Act 2:41) is the New Testament order, and the 1689 Confession holds believer's baptism by immersion. On the oath and the magistracy it stands with Bern: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1) is not suspended for Christians, and the civil office is lawful for a believer. The Zofingen record is therefore a debate in which the dictionary agrees with each party against the other, and with neither about the sword.

pos: n. (Bernese town at the head of Lake Thun; the gate of the Oberland, which rose against the Reformation in 1528)
etymology: German Thun, from Celtic dunum, a fortified hill; the town stands where the Aare leaves the lake under the castle rock.
biblical_def: Thun stands where the Aare leaves its lake, at the entrance of the Bernese Oberland, and it was a governor's seat of the city of Bern and the gate through which Bern's authority reached the high valleys. Those valleys did not want the Reformation. When the mandate of February 1528 abolished the Mass, the Oberland communes—Hasli, Frutigen, the Simmental, Interlaken, Unterseen—refused it, petitioned, and then rose in arms, in a rebellion which Bern put down with troops in the summer of 1528 before enforcing the mandate at the point of its authority. The reasons were mixed, as they always are: a genuine attachment to the old worship and its feasts, a dislike of the city's government, the loss of the Interlaken monastery's charity and employment, and the resentment of mountain communes at being legislated for by patricians in a town. The dictionary enters Thun because the Oberland rising is the part of the Swiss Reformation that the Reformed accounts pass over quickly. A doctrine the dictionary believes to be true was imposed on a people who did not want it, by soldiers, and the soldiers were on the right side of the doctrine and were still soldiers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rising as an insurrection; a mandate as an authoritative command; and compulsion as the act of driving or urging by force.
webster_full: RISING, n. The act of getting up; an insurrection; a sedition; a tumultuous assembly.
MANDATE, n. A command; an authoritative order or injunction; a commission.
COMPULSION, n. [L. compulsio.] The act of driving or urging by force, physical or moral; constraint of the will.
COMMUNE, n. In foreign use, a small territorial district which governs its own local affairs.
PATRICIAN, n. [L. patricius.] A nobleman; in the Swiss and Italian cities, a member of the governing families.

corruption_summary: Bernese town at the gate of the Oberland, whose high valleys refused the Reformation mandate of 1528 and were brought to it by troops.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the compelled conscience, and the dictionary names it here against the side it otherwise agrees with. Bern was right that the Mass is not a sacrifice and that the images had to go; it was wrong to put the question to a people and then, when they answered no, send soldiers. A faith established by force is not established at all, and the Oberland remained the part of the Bernese territory where the old religion was longest regretted and the city's ministers were least trusted.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the only lawful instrument for changing a people's religion is preaching. “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) is the whole of the commission and it contains no clause about troops. “Put up again thy sword into his place” (Mat 26:52) was said to a disciple defending the right side in the plainest case there has ever been or will be, and the dictionary takes it as the rule for every case since.

pos: n. (Bernese town at the mouth of the Emmental; a governor's seat and the school town of the valley)
etymology: German Burgdorf, the castle village, from Burg, a fortified place, and Dorf, a village; the town is built below the Zahringen castle on the Emme.
biblical_def: Burgdorf stands at the mouth of the Emmental, where the long farming valley opens on the Bernese plain, and under the city it was a governor's seat, a market, and the school town for a district of scattered farms. Its church history is the history of the Bernese parish system working in the countryside: a Latin school in the town preparing a few boys for Bern and the ministry, a German school teaching reading and the catechism, the chapter of the district's ministers meeting here for the examination of candidates and the exercise of preaching, and the morals court sitting with the pastor and the elders to deal with the ordinary business of a rural parish. It was this machinery, rather than any great preacher, which made the Emmental one of the most thoroughly Reformed populations in Europe—and which, a century later, made it the valley where the Anabaptists were most stubbornly rooted and most severely hunted, since a catechised farmer who concludes that his catechism is wrong is a far more formidable dissenter than an ignorant one. The dictionary enters Burgdorf for that double result, which the Bernese authorities never understood and which is instructive to anyone who wants a taught people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chapter as an assembly of clergymen; a catechism as instruction by question and answer; and dissent as a differing in opinion, a separation from an established church.
webster_full: CHAPTER, n. [L. capitulum.] A society of clergymen belonging to a cathedral or collegiate church; an assembly of such persons.
CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
DISSENT, n. Difference of opinion; disagreement; a differing or separation from an established church.
EXERCISE, n. Practice; use; the performance of a duty; a public trial of skill, as a sermon preached before a chapter.
ROOTED, adj. Fixed; deep; radical; firmly implanted, as a rooted opinion.

corruption_summary: Bernese town at the mouth of the Emmental whose schools and chapter produced the most thoroughly catechised and the most stubbornly dissenting peasantry in the canton.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the use of catechising as a method of control, which is how the Bernese authorities came to regard it and which is why they were so angry at the result. A catechism is a summary of doctrine put into a form a child can hold; it is not a loyalty oath, and a people trained to give reasons will eventually ask for them. The Emmental's Anabaptists were the city's own schools' doing, and the city hunted them for a century.

The principle to recover is that teaching a people carries a risk the church must accept. “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) is commended of a congregation examining an apostle, and a church which will not be examined has no business catechising anybody. The dictionary holds that a taught people who sometimes dissent is better than an untaught people who always conform, and that the Bernese magistrate's remedy—the sword against the dissenters—was both wicked and an admission that the argument had been lost.

pos: n. (town at the head of Lake Neuchatel in the Pays de Vaud; reformed under Bern after the conquest of 1536)
etymology: French Yverdon, from Latin Eburodunum, the fort of the yew trees, from Celtic eburos, a yew, and dunum, a stronghold.
biblical_def: Yverdon stands at the southern end of Lake Neuchatel, on the old Roman road, and it was one of the chief towns of the Pays de Vaud which Bern took from the duke of Savoy in the winter of 1536. The Bernese brought the Reformation with them, by the method they had used at home: a public disputation—held at Lausanne in October 1536, with Farel and Viret and the young Calvin among those who argued for the Reformed side—and then a mandate abolishing the Mass throughout the conquered country. Yverdon received a Reformed minister, its religious houses were suppressed, and it became the seat of a Bernese governor and of a class of the Vaud ministry. The whole operation took months, and the dictionary states plainly what it was: the religion of a French-speaking Catholic province was changed by the decree of a German-speaking conqueror within a year of the conquest. That the doctrine so imposed was the true doctrine is the dictionary's settled judgment and does not alter the character of the act. The Vaud was Reformed thereafter, and it was a hundred years before its church was anything more than Bern's establishment in a subject land.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conquest as the act of subduing by force; a mandate as an authoritative order; and a subject province as a country held in dependence.
webster_full: CONQUEST, n. [L. conquisitus.] The act of conquering; the subjugation of a country or people by force of arms; that which is conquered.
MANDATE, n. A command; an authoritative order or injunction; a commission.
PROVINCE, n. A country belonging to a kingdom or state, either by conquest or colonization; a division of a kingdom.
ESTABLISHMENT, n. The act of establishing; that which is established; the church established by law in a country.
DECREE, n. An order, edict or law made by a superior as a rule to govern inferiors.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: Vaud town reformed by Bernese mandate within a year of the conquest of 1536, after the disputation at Lausanne.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the reformation by conquest. Bern gave the Vaud a disputation, which was more than most conquerors would have done, and then imposed the result by mandate on a population which had had no part in choosing either the disputation or its judges. The dictionary refuses the two easy accounts—that the end justified it, and that the doctrine is therefore suspect—and states both halves: the doctrine was true, and the means were the means of a conqueror.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one that the later history of the Vaud proves. “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2) is slow and it produces a church; a mandate is quick and produces an establishment. The Vaud got a sound confession, parishes, schools and ministers in 1536, and it took the labour of Viret and a century of preaching before it had a church which held that confession because it believed it.

“Put up again thy sword into his place” (Mat 26:52) — a province's religion changed by a conqueror's decree.
“Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith” (Act 14:22) — the century of preaching that made it a church.

pos: n. (town of the Pays de Vaud, German Peterlingen; seat of a great Cluniac priory suppressed at the Reformation)
etymology: French Payerne, from Latin Paterniacum, the estate of Paternus; German Peterlingen is the same name through a Germanic reading.
biblical_def: Payerne grew up around one of the great Cluniac houses of Burgundy, a priory founded in the tenth century under the patronage of the Burgundian royal house and built on a scale which still dominates the town. It was a daughter of Cluny, exempt from the bishop, rich in lands and tithes through the whole region, and by the sixteenth century it was what such houses commonly were: a great endowment administered by a commendatory prior for the benefit of a noble family, with a reduced community and a good deal of litigation. When Bern took the Vaud in 1536 the priory was suppressed with the rest, its revenues taken into the Bernese treasury and applied in part to the ministry, the schools and the poor of the district. The church became the town's Reformed parish church and part of the monastic buildings served the governor. The dictionary enters Payerne because the suppression of the religious houses is the part of the Reformation most easily caricatured in either direction, and it can be stated accurately here: a rich foundation had long since ceased to do the work it had been given its wealth for, and the Reformation's claim was that the endowment should be spent on preaching, teaching and the poor instead.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a priory as a religious house governed by a prior; commendam as the holding of a benefice in trust; and an endowment as a permanent fund settled for support.
webster_full: PRIORY, n. A convent of which a prior is the superior; in dignity below an abbey; a religious house.
COMMENDAM, n. In ecclesiastical law, a benefice or living commended to the care of a clerk until it should be provided with a regular incumbent.
ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of a church, school or charity; the fund so settled.
TITHE, n. [Sax. teotha.] The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy.
SUPPRESS, v.t. To put an end to; to abolish; to dissolve, as a religious house.
scriptures: Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Pro 9:9
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
corruption_summary: Vaud town whose great Cluniac priory, long held in commendam, was suppressed in 1536 and its revenues turned to the ministry, schools and poor.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the benefice held for the income and not the work: a house with the revenues of a province, a prior appointed because his family wanted the rent, and a community too small to keep the offices it existed to keep. “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2) is the apostolic test of a man who takes charge of souls, and a system which made great ecclesiastical incomes the property of noble houses had put that test beyond application.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the proper use of a church's wealth, and the dictionary states it without pretending the Reformation always observed it. The claim at Payerne was that the endowment should pay for preachers, schools and the poor; where that was done, as in part it was at Bern, the claim was honoured, and where the revenues went to a treasury and thence to a war, it was not. A reformation which takes a corrupt endowment and spends it no better has only changed the beneficiary.

pos: n. (Bernese town on Lake Geneva in the Pays de Vaud; a seat of the colloquies of the Vaud ministry)
etymology: French Morges, from a pre-Latin water-name, the river Morges; the town was founded by the house of Savoy about 1286 on the lake shore.
biblical_def: Morges is a lake town of the Vaud between Lausanne and Geneva, a Bernese bailliage after 1536 and one of the places where the colloquies of the Vaud ministry met. Those gatherings are the reason for the entry, because they were the body in which the Vaud's ministers pressed, for twenty years, the question that broke them. The Bernese church order kept discipline in the magistrate's hand: the admission and exclusion of communicants belonged to the council and its officers, and the ministers were instructed that the Supper was not to be refused on their own judgment. Viret at Lausanne, and the Vaud ministers with him, held that the church must be able to exclude the openly scandalous from the table, and that a minister who gives the sacrament to a man he knows to be living in open sin has failed in his charge. They petitioned, argued in colloquy and synod, and in 1558 refused to administer the Supper at Christmas without the discipline. Bern deposed and banished them in 1559; Viret and Beza went to Geneva, and the academy of Lausanne lost its teachers.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colloquy as a conference or mutual discourse; excommunication as the exclusion of a person from the communion of the church; and jurisdiction as legal power or authority.
webster_full: COLLOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a conference, as of ministers in a district.
EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church, or cutting off from the communion of the faithful.
JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; extent of power or authority.
DEPOSE, v.t. [L. depono.] To lay down; to divest of office; to remove from a throne or other high station.
SCANDALOUS, adj. Giving offense; opprobrious; defamatory; disgraceful to reputation, as scandalous conduct.
scriptures: But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Gal 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
corruption_summary: Vaud town of the ministers' colloquies, where the Bernese refusal of church discipline led to the deposition of Viret and the Lausanne ministers in 1559.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the Erastian one: the magistrate holding the keys. Bern's order was not a neglect of discipline—the Bernese morals courts were vigorous—but a transfer of it, so that admission to the Lord's table was a civil administration's decision. “But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup” (1Co 11:28) puts the first duty on the communicant; the church's officers have the second, and a council cannot discharge either.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary holds with Viret, and holds also that discipline is the church's own act through its own officers rather than a presbytery's or a council's. “no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5) is the measure of what the Vaud ministers did in refusing the Supper in 1558, and they paid the ordinary price: deposition, banishment, and the loss to the Vaud of the best teachers it had. Bern won the dispute and spent the next century with a church it had made unable to govern itself.

pos: n. (chief town of the Chablais on Lake Geneva; Reformed under Bern from 1536 and recovered for Rome by the mission of 1594)
etymology: French Thonon, from a pre-Latin root, perhaps Celtic dunum, a fort; the town stands on the south shore of Lake Geneva below the Savoy hills.
biblical_def: Thonon is the chief town of the Chablais, the Savoyard country on the southern shore of Lake Geneva, and it changed its religion twice in sixty years. When Bern overran Savoy in 1536 the Chablais was taken with the Vaud and reformed by mandate; for a generation it had Reformed ministers, and its religious houses were suppressed. In 1564 the treaty of Lausanne returned the Chablais to Savoy, and the duke, unable at first to undo the settlement, left it alone. Then in 1594 the bishop of Geneva, resident at Annecy, sent Francis de Sales and a small mission into the Chablais, with the duke's protection and later his soldiers. Over four years they preached, disputed, printed broadsheets against the Reformed ministers, visited, and held public processions; by 1598 the Chablais was substantially Catholic again, and the Reformed ministry was gone. The dictionary enters Thonon because it is the one episode in this batch in which the Reformed were out-preached. The mission used the methods the Reformation itself had used—vernacular preaching, printed argument, catechising, personal visitation, patience—and the Reformed church of the Chablais, planted by a conqueror's mandate and never rooted in the people, could not answer them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a body of persons sent to propagate religion; a broadside as a sheet printed on one side; and to recover as to regain possession of a thing lost.
webster_full: MISSION, n. A sending or being sent; persons sent to propagate religion; a station of missionaries.
BROADSIDE, n. A sheet of paper containing matter printed on one side only, and intended for general circulation.
RECOVER, v.t. [L. recupero.] To regain; to get or obtain that which was lost; to restore from sickness or depression.
PROCESSION, n. [L. processio.] A train of persons walking or riding in ceremonious solemnity, as in a religious observance.
ROOTED, adj. Fixed; deep; firmly implanted; radical.
scriptures: Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Mat 7:15
Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.
corruption_summary: Chablais town reformed by Bernese mandate in 1536 and recovered for Rome between 1594 and 1598 by a mission that preached, printed and visited.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrines the Chablais mission restored are the doctrines the Reformation called the church away from, and the dictionary names them: the Mass as a sacrifice, the invocation of saints, the authority of the papal see, the veneration of images, and the whole system of merit. That the mission conducted itself largely by argument rather than by the sword does not make its doctrine true, and the duke's soldiers were in the country throughout.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the episode teaches against the Reformed. A church established by mandate and maintained by a foreign magistrate had, after fifty years, no body of catechised and persuaded people to stand on, and it fell to a mission of a few men with a press and a willingness to walk. “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) is the ministry's work, and the Chablais ministers had not done it in a form the people could use. The dictionary takes this as the standing refutation of the territorial method: what a decree establishes, a preacher can take away.
